What it says: for every measurable partition, the vector of probabilities is Dirichlet with parameter $(\alpha(A_1),\dots,\alpha(A_k))$
What it hides: that draws are discrete; existence needs Kolmogorov

What it makes obvious: **almost-sure discreteness**, and the size of the largest atom

What it says: draw $X_n$ from $\alpha+\sum_{i<n}\delta_{X_i}$, normalized; the empirical measure converges to a discrete $P$ distributed as Ferguson's
What it makes obvious: the predictive rule, hence exchangeability and the link to the CRP
What it hides: that $\alpha$ is a measure and not a number, if written carelessly

What it says: customer $n$ joins an occupied table with probability proportional to its size, or a new one with probability proportional to $\alpha(\mathcal{X})$
What it makes obvious: the induced partition, hence $K_J$ and Antoniak's law
What it hides: the random measure entirely — this is the level R2 objected to
